title: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck
description: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the annual Computex trade show in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2026. Tsai Hsin-han | ReutersSINGAPORE — The chief executives o
body: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the annual Computex trade show in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2026. Tsai Hsin-han | ReutersSINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models."[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns."If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said.Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity.The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns.Hock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands."[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now."He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online.Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure."There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply," Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030.Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power.But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said.Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau.Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.

schema.headline: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck

title: Justice Department investigates TV networks as White House press-access fight escalates
description: CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein works in the CNN workspace outside the West Wing of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24, 2026. CNN a
body: CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein works in the CNN workspace outside the West Wing of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24, 2026. CNN and MS NOW said their reporters were allowed back into the White House on Thursday after a judge ordered that their access be restored.Saul Loeb | AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation into whether the White House television press pool's decision to suspend coverage of President Donald Trump violated antitrust laws. The Justice Department said in a statement that it is examining whether the White House TV press pool — a group of broadcasters including CNN, Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC — violated the Sherman Act by temporarily halting pooled TV coverage of Trump.The Sherman Act is a federal law that prohibits certain agreements that unreasonably restrain trade. Introduced in the 1890s, the law has rarely been applied to media organizations, particularly regarding their coverage. Members of the press pool did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment sent outside of normal business hours.  The DOJ investigation follows the White House television press pool ceased its coverage of Trump on Sept. 21, shortly after he prohibited CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House. In a Truth Social post, the president said then that those outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."A judge lifted restrictions on those reporters on Sept. 24, several days after White House staff confiscated their press passes. Despite the ruling, reporters from CNN and Politico were barred from traveling with the president on Air Force One, the New York Times reported.The Trump administration now faces a lawsuit from CNN, MS NOW and Politico over its ban of their reporters from the White House grounds. Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed.The DOJ investigation marks another escalation in an ongoing dispute between Trump and the media over press rights. The Trump administration has moved to restrict news agencies that have produced critical coverage of its policies. Last year, Trump moved to rescind about $1.1 billion previously approved for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, federal funding earmarked for public broadcasters NPR and PBS. Trump and his allies have also sued several media organizations, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and BBC News, over alleged biases or inaccuracies in their reporting.Seth Stern, chief of advocacy for the Freedom of the Press Foundation, called the DOJ investigation "nonsense.""Depriving Trump of the attention he craves is not a competitive harm and in any case, antitrust law has long recognized First Amendment exceptions even when there is anticompetitive impact," he said. "After all his 'fake news' rhetoric, Trump is weaponizing the DOJ to pressure the networks he calls the 'enemy of the people' to stay at the White House. It's a weird way of telling the press how much he missed them."The White House Correspondents' Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

schema.headline: Justice Department investigates TV networks as White House press-access fight escalates

title: I’m a psychologist who studies couples: The No. 1 way to end a fight before it escalates—it works ‘almost immediately’
description: Couples tend to slide off-course when they argue. You might start out talking about something real and specific. Maybe a plan that was altered without
body: Couples tend to slide off-course when they argue. You might start out talking about something real and specific. Maybe a plan that was altered without a check-in or an impulse purchase that should have been discussed. Then suddenly you've stopped talking about that thing and started talking about each other: "Why are you overreacting?""You always do this.""You're being impossible right now."One minute you're trying to solve a problem together, and the next you're each trying to prove you're the more reasonable person in the room. And once an argument becomes about that, it can't really be resolved. Because now, the battlefield and ammunition are endless.As a psychologist who studies couples, I know that, thankfully, there's a practice that can act as a guardrail for disagreements. I call it a partial yield, and it prevents this all-too-familiar detour.What a 'partial yield' sounds likeA partial yield is a type of phrase you use when you concede the specific piece of the argument you're genuinely responsible for, the moment it comes up, without conceding the rest of your position. It usually sounds very ordinary:"You're right, that part's on me." "That's fair, I did forget to tell you." "I shouldn't have made that decision without talking to you first." So you're not agreeing that you were wrong about everything. But you are admitting the fault that's actually yours, before your partner has to pry it out of you.In my experience, nothing de-escalates a conflict faster.Why a 'partial yield' works so quicklyWhen your partner confronts you, some part of them is preemptively braced for the effort of convincing you. It's why voices get louder and why examples start piling up. They're not trying to hurt you. They're trying to get you to believe them, and they've assumed it's going to be hard.A partial yield releases the pent-up steam that can otherwise fuel an escalation. The effect is palpable almost immediately, and it rarely feels like a defeat for either person. Your partner gets the acknowledgment they were pushing for, and you get to be honest about your part without signing away the rest.It's also easier on you than a full apology, which matters more than you might think. Most of us don't withhold small admissions because we believe we did nothing wrong. We withhold them because admitting to one thing feels like admitting to all the rest, too, and we'd rather concede nothing than concede everything. What happens when you skip this stepI'd pay attention to what happens when you don't use a partial yield phrase.If you never take accountability in the moment, the problem doesn't just go away. Your partner notices and files it away. They might bring it up again three weeks from now in the middle of an unrelated argument. It may look like score-keeping, but more often it's an old grievance that never got heard and owned, finally finding an opening.Couples who concede small things routinely don't build up much of that "back-pocket" inventory, so there's nothing to reach for at a moment's notice. Their arguments tend to stay roughly within the context of whatever caused them.How to use the 'partial yield' effectivelyA few steps differentiate a real partial yield from a fake one:Be specific about what you're claiming. "You're right, I shouldn't have said it like that in front of your mom," works. A vague "Okay, fine, I was wrong!" reads as surrender under protest, and your partner will hear it that way.Don't attach a "but." "You're right, that part's on me, but you also…" cancels the whole thing. If you have a counterpoint, it will survive the next 90 seconds. Let the concession stand alone first.Do it early. The yield loses most of its power once someone has already started listing their old grievances. The ideal moment is the first time you notice you're technically in the wrong about something small, which is usually much earlier than we like to admit.Say it even when you're mostly right. Especially then. Being mostly right is the most common reason people refuse to concede anything at all.In my experience, genuine partial yields are the difference between couples who argue about — and solve — problems and couples who get stuck arguing about each other.Mark Travers, Ph.D., is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the lead psychologist at Awake Therapy, a telehealth company that provides online psychotherapy, counseling and coaching. He is also the curator of the popular mental health and wellness website Therapytips.org.

schema.headline: I’m a psychologist who studies couples: The No. 1 way to end a fight before it escalates—it works ‘almost immediately’

title: Trump Media advisor Katie Zacharia named White House press secretary
description: Katie Zacharia attends the Nashville premiere of 'David' at AMC DINE-IN Thoroughbred 20 on December 14, 2025 in Franklin, Tennessee.Terry Wyatt | Gett
body: Katie Zacharia attends the Nashville premiere of 'David' at AMC DINE-IN Thoroughbred 20 on December 14, 2025 in Franklin, Tennessee.Terry Wyatt | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Sunday named Katie Zacharia, a lawyer and conservative commentator at Trump Media & Technology, to be the next White House press secretary."I am pleased to announce that Katie Zacharia will be beginning her term as Press Secretary tomorrow, Columbus Day, and will be doing an introductory News Conference on Tuesday at 9:30 A.M. from the Press Briefing Room in the White House," the president wrote in a Truth Social post. "Katie has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning, and will do a fantastic job!" he added.Zacharia, a self-described "hardline Trump supporter," succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Leavitt went on maternity leave after giving birth to her second child earlier this year. She is expected to join Fox News as an on-air contributor next month.According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia has worked since June as a senior communications advisor for Trump Media, which owns the president's preferred social media outlet, Truth Social.Her profile also shows that she serves as general counsel at Fix California, a conservative activist group founded by Richard Grenell, Trump's special presidential envoy for special missions and former head of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.In March, Zacharia finished a two-month stint as a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security, according to her LinkedIn page.Zacharia's IMDb page lists dozens of appearances on Fox News political talk shows and other conservative outlets.— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Trump Media advisor Katie Zacharia named White House press secretary

title: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
description: Shoppers gather at New Market in Kolkata, India, on September 21, 2026, ahead of the Durga Puja festival. Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesIndia's he
body: Shoppers gather at New Market in Kolkata, India, on September 21, 2026, ahead of the Durga Puja festival. Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesIndia's headline inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August, adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy.The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%, according to a Reuters poll. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in the world's fastest-growing economy and has touched a 22-month high in September.India's food inflation climbed 7.74% in September from 5.97% the month prior, with prices rising faster in rural areas than cities, India's Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation said in a Monday release. Transport services for goods inflation rose 14.73% while that for personal transport jumped 7.46%, as per the release.Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023, joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy in a bid to arrest accelerating inflation. India's central bank also said that in the "current conditions" further rate cuts were "off the table in the near term" and policy action could either be a rate hike or a pause.Inflation risks mountIndia is among the countries most vulnerable to the supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. It imports nearly 85% of its fuel needs, and before the Iran war it heavily relied on energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices have been elevated due to the tensions in the Middle East. Experts, however, predict that prices will remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias.India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, which is higher than the RBI's medium-term target of 4%. The RBI raised India's economic growth estimate by 40 basis points to 7.1% but cautioned that protracted geopolitical tensions, trade frictions, tightening of financial conditions and elevated international commodity prices would likely weigh on economic activity.Food prices in particular and India's rural economy also face an added risk from the Super El Nino, with the country receiving its lowest rainfall in over a decade during June to September, a key season for its largely rain-fed farms and reservoirs. The rainfall was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme drought conditions.HSBC said in a report on Oct. 7 that it expects another rate hike in December, a day after the RBI policy action. "This may not be a deep tightening cycle, but a tightening cycle it is," the analysts said, adding that the September retail inflation data is likely to show a "sizeable headline pop."

schema.headline: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates

title: Judge orders Trump administration to immediately stop taxpayer-funded TV ads
description: US President Donald Trump speaks during a Columbus Day celebration in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2026. Alex Wro
body: US President Donald Trump speaks during a Columbus Day celebration in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2026. Alex Wroblewski | Afp | Getty ImagesA federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing controversial government-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump that critics call political propaganda intended to influence the November midterm election.The temporary restraining order by Judge Jennifer Rochon in Manhattan federal court also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more of the $20 million allocated for the ad campaign. About $19 million of that allocation has already been spent on the ads.The order came a day after the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office, which is defending the Trump administration in a lawsuit challenging the ads, told Rochon the ads would not continue airing past Sunday. Rochon's order, which lasts 14 days unless extended, directs the Trump administration to cancel all scheduled ads, including those due to air on Sunday evening. The ads have included the caption "Paid for by the U.S. Government" since they began being aired.The Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office declined to comment. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.Congress appropriated the money for the ads for immigration enforcement.The coalition of plaintiffs that sued to block the ads told Rochon earlier Sunday that she should issue the TRO despite the U.S. Attorney's Office's claim that the ads would not continue past Sunday."Defendants admit that appropriated funds were used to pay for political ads and do not disputethat this use of taxpayer money is unlawful," the plaintiffs said in a court filing Sunday. "Instead, much of Defendants' opposition boils down to a single premise: it is too late for the Court to act. That is not because Defendants have stopped airing the ads," the plaintiffs said. "Indeed, Defendants assert — boldly, given their failure to defend the ads on the merits — that ads will continue to air today, including during evening programming that will attract millions of viewers."Rochon agreed, saying in her order that the U.S. Attorney's statement that the ads would stop Sunday did not render the TRO request moot. The judge also rejected the Justice Department's argument that the coalition lacked legal standing to challenge the ads.Rochon said the coalition has shown it is likely to win the lawsuit, would suffer irreparable harm if the TRO is not granted, and that "an injunction serves the public interest."In addition, the judge ordered the Trump administration not to enter into any new agreements or expand existing ones for the ads. And she stayed a purchase order for the ads between U.S. Customs and Border Protection and a contractor, Lepugh Inc., doing business as LMD Agency Inc.Rochon said she would soon issue a full opinion explaining her ruling.The coalition, which filed its lawsuit on Oct. 7, includes the advocacy group Common Cause and the Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, which is headquartered in New York City.The Democratic National Committee filed a separate lawsuit challenging the ads that same day. The ads, which have aired for weeks, drew criticism from Democrats who said they seem designed to help Trump's fellow Republicans in November's election, which will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress.In its lawsuit, the coalition described one ad, titled "The Country He Loves," as featuring "rapid cuts of photos and videos of President Trump mixed in with text touting what the President views as his accomplishments in office," which includes "Largest Tax Cuts in History;" "Reigniting American Manufacturing;" and "Defend Law and Order and Police.""Between those messages, the screen repeatedly flashes the words "AMERICA WILL NEVER BE A COMMUNIST COUNTRY," the civil complaint noted.Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., wrote White House chief of staff Susie Wiles on Sept. 24, a day after that ad first aired."The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates,'" Hassan wrote.Trump, in response to that criticism, said on Oct. 5 that, going forward, he or his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for the ads. The White House later said the president would not reimburse the federal government for the cost of the ads that had already aired.In a statement Sunday evening on Rochon's order, the coalition said, "We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.""There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the coalition said, referring to Trump."As this case moves forward and voters make their voices heard in this election, we will work to ensure the rule of law continues to be upheld, protecting the rights of voters and our democracy."

schema.headline: Judge orders Trump administration to immediately stop taxpayer-funded TV ads

title: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
description: Vice President JD Vance speaks alongside, from left to right, White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller, U.S. Att
body: Vice President JD Vance speaks alongside, from left to right, White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito, and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson during a press conference regarding a federal investigation alleging fraud and abuse of the H-1B visa program, in Washington, Oct. 8, 2026.Alex Wroblewski | AFP | Getty ImagesAs the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft, claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas. The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers.Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended.The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad.Who's on the listAll eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45.The biggest sponsor wasn't suspendedAmazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals.If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. ... Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them.JD VanceVice President of the United StatesWhat the numbers showThe numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

schema.headline: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows

title: Global travel warnings after Iran-backed Houthi militants strike Riyadh airport
description: An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sept. 19, 2026.AFP | Getty ImagesSaudi Arabia said Monday it wa
body: An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sept. 19, 2026.AFP | Getty ImagesSaudi Arabia said Monday it was dealing with more drones and missile strikes as a slew of countries warned against travel to the Kingdom due to fatal attacks on Riyadh airport by Iran-backed Houthi militants.The Australian and New Zealand governments on Monday cautioned their citizens against traveling to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and other Saudi destinations, joining similar advisories from the U.K., U.S., Canada, France, Germany, Japan and others. It came as the Saudi aviation authority extended the suspension of operations at the airport, which has been hit by numerous projectiles over the last week. The deadliest strike came on Saturday, when 12 people were killed and more than 300 were injured, according to officials. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and injured nearly a dozen. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which have raised questions over the robustness of Saudi Arabia's defense capabilities despite its huge military spending. The fatalities come as the Kingdom hosts major corporate conferences, including the World ⁠Petroleum Congress, the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting and the Future Investment Initiative.Surveillance footage shows smoke and fire at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 10, 2026, in this frame from a handout video.Saudi Ministry of Media | ReutersU.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the U.S. "may" join Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against the Houthis.Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that he had told Saudi Arabian Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud by phone that Tehran was willing to take steps to start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, where the Houthis are based. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei meanwhile said that Iran was still reviewing a U.S. response to its proposal for reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and would reply though its intermediaries, Reuters reported.

schema.headline: Global travel warnings after Iran-backed Houthi militants strike Riyadh airport

title: Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an ‘emergency brake’ that humans control
description: Satya Nadella, chief executive officer of Microsoft Corp., during an event in San Francisco, California, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. David Paul Mo
body: Satya Nadella, chief executive officer of Microsoft Corp., during an event in San Francisco, California, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMicrosoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake" that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task."We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient,"  Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X."Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system," he said. Nadella's comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast. An AI researcher quit Anthropic last month and accused the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of "gambling with our lives." Later that day, an alignment lead at Anthropic focused on AI safety said there's a greater than 10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans" within the next decade.Conversely, President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed AI extinction risks and has instead emphasized that the industry needs to stay ahead of China. Trump also recently introduced a new "AI Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors. Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability." They include model diversity; a human-readable footprint of the model's actions; continuous system testing; independent controls and auditability; containment; and incident disclosure, Nadella wrote. "The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most," he wrote. "It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least."

schema.headline: Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an ‘emergency brake’ that humans control

title: Why Japan's 7-Eleven store closures in India don’t signal an exit
description: 7-Eleven & i Holdings logo is seen in Tokyo, Japan on March 19, 2026. (Photo by Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty I
body: 7-Eleven & i Holdings logo is seen in Tokyo, Japan on March 19, 2026. (Photo by Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesJapanese convenience store chain 7-Eleven's second attempt to crack India's retail market through a franchise model may have failed, but the company has no plans to write off its ambitions to build a presence in one of the world's most populous countries.At the end of September, Reliance Retail, the master franchise operator of 7-Eleven stores, shut down all 31 outlets across India, a spokesperson for the Japanese company told CNBC in an email. Reliance Retail is owned by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries.The 7-Eleven representative said that the company still aspires to serve customers in India and "looks forward to exploring several options to advance our presence in the market over the long term."The spokesperson declined to provide additional comments on Reliance's business decisions and the status of the agreement between the Japanese and Indian companies. Reliance Retail did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment.The two firms had announced their partnership in 2021, after the Japanese company's pact with another Indian company, Future Retail, was terminated. At the time, Future Retail, in a regulatory disclosure, had said the termination was mutual as it was "not able to meet the target of opening stores and payment of franchisee fees."Analysts told CNBC that the 7-Eleven store closures point to a reset of its operations in India, not to an exit, especially at a time when its rival Japanese chain Lawsons has also made plans to enter India. The closures do not mean that "7-Eleven is giving up on India," Sohrab Bararia, partner at consultancy firm Grant Thornton Bharat, told CNBC. "It seems more like a rethink of the current franchise arrangement, particularly given the losses under the existing model," he added.7-India Convenience Retail, a wholly owned subsidiary of Reliance Retail that entered into a master franchise agreement with 7-Eleven in 2021, reported a net loss of nearly 900 million rupees ($9.3 million) in the year ended March 2026 on revenues of around 920 million rupees. The firm's losses have widened continuously from 52 million rupees in the financial year ended March 2022, as per data from Tracxn.The ChallengesCreating a compelling reason to visit a convenience store is a big challenge for small-format outlets in India, experts said. While larger stores offer lower prices and experiential shopping with a wide variety of products, smaller stores with limited inventory struggle to compete. Meanwhile, 10-minute-delivery grocery apps are growing in popularity as they have a wider selection and offer convenience, which customers in big cities prefer, experts said."Small-format stores, meanwhile, bear high rents and full staffing costs but generate relatively low sales per outlet," Bharat Birla, executive director of Anand Rathi Investment Banking, told CNBC.However, analysts said that even though India's convenience store market is crowded with 10-minute-delivery apps and small mom-and-pop shops, Japanese companies could still find a niche that diversifies away from a "traditional grocery-led model."Lawson's plans to establish a "local subsidiary and operate directly managed stores from 2027," Birla said, adding that 7-Eleven could also consider this route. Earlier this year, multiple Japanese media reports said the convenience store chain plans to open its first five stores in Mumbai in 2027 and plans to have a total of 100 stores in India by 2030. These stores will be owned and managed through a local subsidiary that Lawson will set up in India before February 2027, the reports said. A shift away from the twice-failed franchise model would provide 7-Eleven with room for "strategic involvement" while allowing for localization and a broader pathway to scale across India, Bararia said.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconReliance Industries share price, Indian rupees

schema.headline: Why Japan's 7-Eleven store closures in India don’t signal an exit

title: Brent tops $105 as doubts grow over supply boost from Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’
description: Oil prices reversed initial losses early Monday, despite the potential for improved supplies after U.S. President Donald Trump declared an "energy cea
body: Oil prices reversed initial losses early Monday, despite the potential for improved supplies after U.S. President Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery rose 0.92% $105.68 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November ticked 0.95% higher to $92.72 per barrel. Prices on both benchmarks had fallen by around 1.5% earlier in the session."Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump said in a social media statement Sunday stateside.Oil reversed its losses after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed such a ceasefire, but warned Monday that Moscow must do the same. Prospects of more Russian energy hitting markets after a deal with the U.S. have also risen after Trump said Friday that Moscow will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under a deal he struck with Putin during a phone call.Elsewhere early on Monday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said it was dealing with another round of drones and missiles attacks directed at Saudi Arabia.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon BrentIt comes after Iran's Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi made a phone call to Saudi Arabia's Minister of Foreign Affairs Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah to discuss the region's recent escalation of events as well as the efforts to address it, according to the Saudi state news agency,Al Jazeera reported Araghchi had said Iran was ready to provide assistance to help with the start of dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis. Stock Chart IconStock chart icon wtiOil prices are expected to remain volatile in the near term as the U.S.-Iran conflict continues, while the impact of Hurricane Isaias on U.S. energy producers could also hurt supplies . "The pressure on oil prices could remain on the upside as Hurricane Isaias strengthened to Category 3 with 120mph winds as it approached the US Gulf Coast, forcing energy producers to curtail offshore output," UOB said in a note on Monday. "Separately, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport on Sat which killed 12 people and injured over 300, have materially elevated Middle East risk premia," UOB added.

schema.headline: Brent tops $105 as doubts grow over supply boost from Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’

title: Nobel prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford
description: Secretary General of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Ellen Moons (C), Chair of the Prize Committee John Hassler (L) and Member of the Prize Comm
body: Secretary General of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Ellen Moons (C), Chair of the Prize Committee John Hassler (L) and Member of the Prize Committee and expert Timo Boppart announce U.S. economists Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford as the winners of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on October 12, 2026.Jonathan Nackstrand | Afp | Getty ImagesRobert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were on Monday awarded the Nobel prize in economics for work that underpins the models used by central banks and governments to stabilize periods of boom and bust.The U.S.-born pair were jointly awarded for their contribution to the "microeconomic foundations" needed to create macroeconomic stability. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was established by Sweden's central bank in 1968. The winners will split a 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) prize. Hall, born in California, is a professor at Stanford University, while Massachusetts-born Woodford is a professor at Columbia University."With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement. Instead of just looking at macroeconomic variables such as  inflation, production and consumption, Hall and Woodford showed how the combined effect of individual households and businesses affects the economy through their forward-looking decision making, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said in a statement. They also demonstrated how central bank and government communications "influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction," the Academy said. "On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy's peaks and troughs," the Academy added."Since the new models' introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us."The economics memorial prize is the last to be announced, following the original Nobels in Physiology or Medicine, Physics, Chemistry, Literature and Peace.This year's laureates include Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work promoting peace and international law, and Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson, who won the Literature prize for a "bold and inventive oeuvre."

schema.headline: Nobel prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford

title: AI FOMO driving some family offices into tech investments, survey suggests
description: Nattrass | E+ | Getty ImagesA version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and c
body: Nattrass | E+ | Getty ImagesA version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.Eighty-five percent of family offices rank artificial intelligence as their top investment theme, despite 75% expecting an AI bubble to burst within the next five years, according to a new survey. The poll of 155 North American family offices was conducted by RBC Wealth Management and Campden Wealth.RBC's Bill Ringham said these mixed feelings about AI can be traced to several potential factors, including cautious optimism about the technology and concerns about sitting on the sidelines of an investment boom."Even patient capital can be caught up in the fear of missing out," said the director of private wealth strategies.A combined 85% of respondents ranked AI an asset class or investment theme likely to reward investors over the next 12 months, the next two to five years, or both. The next most popular picks were U.S. equities and direct investments, selected by 76% and 72% of respondents, respectively.However, while AI was the top investment theme of 2026 at 59%, family offices said they were more bullish on U.S. equities in the long run. When asked about returns over the next two to five years, 69% of respondents chose U.S. equities compared to 64% for AI. Direct investments closely followed at 62%. And while only 26% of family offices said real estate was likely to reward shareholders over the next 12 months, nearly twice as many (51%) picked it as a rewarding investment in the two- to five-year horizon.Ringham said the results may reflect how AI enthusiasm is influencing investors' short-term focus more than their long-term strategy."Fear of missing out is a short-term view," he said. "You're seeing AI over the next 12 months as being that top priority. Their long-term look swings back."Ringham said family offices were cautiously optimistic about AI, especially in the startup space. "Those optimists are also not afraid to say that there might be a bubble down the road," he said. "You're investing in what you think is going to be incredibly successful in the longer term. But at this stage, there are so many new companies that you really have to go into these things with your eyes wide open."The survey found that 76% of respondents ranked "excessive government borrowing" as the top market risk likely to crystallize over the next five years. That was followed by "AI investment bubble burst" (75%) and "AI advancements impact employment" (66%).While the survey did not ask how family offices planned to change their allocations around AI, Ringham said that many asset classes are touched by the technology. 31% of family offices planned to make more direct investments in private equity and just over a fifth said the same of real estate and venture capital, respectively. "I'm sure AI is embedded in a lot of those underlying categories," he said.

schema.headline: AI FOMO driving some family offices into tech investments, survey suggests

title: TikTok CEO sees major scientific breakthroughs from AI within three years
description: TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew.Olivier Douliery | AFP | Getty ImagesSINGAPORE — TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew expects artificial intelligence to drive major scient
body: TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew.Olivier Douliery | AFP | Getty ImagesSINGAPORE — TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew expects artificial intelligence to drive major scientific breakthroughs within the next three years, transforming a broad range of sectors."In the next two to three years, we're going to have a real scientific breakthrough: physics, biotech, chemistry, material science, because of AI. It's very, very, very possible," Chew said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.Chew's remarks come as ByteDance, TikTok's Chinese parent, expands its artificial intelligence research beyond consumer applications. In April, the company's Seed research team unveiled Protenix-v2, an AI model focused on biomolecular structure prediction and design, with potential applications in drug discovery. Chew said rapid advances in AI were opening up possibilities far beyond the technology's current applications, even as questions remain over how to ensure increasingly powerful systems operate within human ethical boundaries."If that happens, then you know the question would be: how do you align the models? How do you align the machines to be doing things that are obvious to us as human beings?" he said.Chew highlighted the accelerating pace of technological development, particularly in scientific research, arguing that the longer-term implications of AI could be far greater than currently anticipated. "The trend is very very clear. It's that we are only at the beginning of what artificial intelligence can probably do," he said. "And if you look at where the trend is, [where] the progress is, particularly in areas of science, it's really trending on a very steep curve at this moment in time."Chew explained that while the technology's immediate impact could be overstated, its longer-term potential remained underappreciated. "I think in the short term we are probably overestimating it, but in the long term we are probably underestimating it," he said.His optimism comes at a time when technology giants have been pouring billions of dollars into AI-powered scientific research. Last week, the U.S. government, Meta and Google announced their participation in a $1.8 billion initiative to develop AI models capable of predicting how cells behave, in an effort to accelerate biological research and drug discovery.TikTok's parent company, ByteDance, is also developing its own AI models and exploring opportunities to collaborate with scientists on research."There's an effort to see how we can collaborate with a lot of scientists to make some progress in science as well," Chew added. "There's been some work that we've done in this area, and it is very exciting."He described scientific discovery as one of the most promising applications of AI, even as the technology increasingly reshapes TikTok's operations, from content creation and recommendations to search and moderation.Chew cautioned that AI's growing capabilities would require stronger safeguards, particularly as autonomous systems become more widely adopted."I think the cybersecurity risks are quite big," he said, warning that users may grant AI agents extensive permissions without fully understanding the potential consequences.He pointed to the risks of allowing AI agents to make purchases autonomously, saying the systems could end up buying more than users intended in their eagerness to complete a task.Chew also highlighted the growing cybersecurity challenges facing companies, as increasingly sophisticated AI models make it significantly cheaper for malicious actors to carry out fraudulent activities."So you need the right tools to now you know defend against the fast falling cost of creating problems for platforms like us, security problems for us," he emphasized.

schema.headline: TikTok CEO sees major scientific breakthroughs from AI within three years

title: Tokenization could unleash tens of billions of dollars in trapped capital, Nasdaq CEO says
description: Attendees at the Token2049 conference in Singapore, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. The crypto conference runs through today. Photographer: Ore Huiying/Blo
body: Attendees at the Token2049 conference in Singapore, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. The crypto conference runs through today. Photographer: Ore Huiying/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesTokenization could free up tens of billions of dollars in capital tied up in assets used as collateral across the global financial system, Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman said.Tokenizing assets such as Treasurys, equities and money market funds, along with the flow of money, could make collateral more liquid, Friedman told CNBC's Joanna Ossinger at the TOKEN2049 conference in Singapore."If you tokenize all those instruments along with the flow of money, then the collateral becomes very fluid," Friedman said.Tokenization involves representing financial assets, such as stocks and bonds, as digital tokens that can be transferred using blockchain technology.Friedman said institutional interest in tokenization has grown over the past year, pointing in part to the passage of the Genius Act in the U.S., which established a regulatory framework for stablecoins."If we can tokenize money, then we can tokenize the flow of capital," she said.That growing institutional interest is converging with demand from retail investors, who have long sought the ability to trade around the clock, according to Friedman. The retail ecosystem "has been about 10 years ahead," she said.The push toward 24/7 tradingMoving to a fully 24/7 market would be a major undertaking for the financial industry, Friedman said."The easiest part is the exchange infrastructure," she said.Friedman said that financial institutions have traditionally had periods when markets are closed to update systems and manage risk. But operating around the clock would require those processes, including risk and collateral management, to take place continuously."Everything has to be real time all the time," she said.Artificial intelligence could help financial institutions manage that transition. Nasdaq has launched a series of digital agents within its risk management platform that initially provide recommendations, Friedman said.Over time, banks could use those agents to take more direct action, she added."AI is critical for 24/7," Friedman said.Bridging crypto and traditional financeCompanies outside the U.S. are showing interest in tokenization and access to American capital markets, Arjun Sethi, co-CEO of cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, told CNBC.Sethi pointed to a company generating roughly $25 million in revenue that was exploring ways to access capital markets, as well as larger international companies interested in tokenization and U.S. public listings.He said tokenization could help expand access to capital markets for companies around the world.However, round-the-clock trading may not be suitable for everything, according to Friedman."Not every asset is liquid enough to support a 24/7 environment," she said. Still, greater connectivity across the global financial system could also open up access to asset classes that were previously out of reach for some investors, Friedman said.

schema.headline: Tokenization could unleash tens of billions of dollars in trapped capital, Nasdaq CEO says
